name: Apache Camel
summary: A Java integration framework that moves and transforms messages between systems with routes built from Enterprise Integration Patterns, written in Java, XML or YAML, with over 350 connectors.
intro: Camel is a library, not a server: it runs inside your Java application, a Spring Boot or Quarkus service, or from the `camel` command line built on JBang. A CamelContext holds routes. Each route has exactly one input endpoint and any number of outputs, and endpoints are written as URIs such as `kafka:orders`, `aws2-s3://bucket`, `jms:queue:invoices` or `timer:tick?period=1s`; the part before the colon picks a component, the plugin that knows how to talk to that system. Between input and output, processors implement the Enterprise Integration Patterns from Hohpe and Woolf’s 2003 book: content-based routers, message filters, splitters, aggregators, content enrichers, idempotent consumers, dead-letter channels and dozens more, each with the same name in every DSL. Pluggable data formats convert message bodies, and expression languages such as Simple read headers and bodies.

Where NiFi gives you a drawn graph on a server, Camel gives you code that lives in your repository and deploys like any other service. Around the core sit Camel Spring Boot and Camel Quarkus for running routes as microservices, Kamelets (reusable, parameterised route snippets used as connectors), the Camel Kafka Connector, which exposes Camel components as Kafka Connect connectors, Camel K for running integrations on Kubernetes, and Karavan, a visual designer for routes. Camel 4.23.0 came out in October 2026 and runs on Java 17, 21 or 25; 4.22 and 4.18 are long-term-support lines.
strengths: A very large catalogue of components, from HTTP, JMS, Kafka and S3 to SaaS APIs, files and databases, all used through the same URI and route model
Integration patterns such as splitting, aggregation, retries and dead-letter handling come built in, with consistent names across Java, XML and YAML
Routes are code: they live in Git, are reviewed and unit-tested, and run inside an ordinary Spring Boot or Quarkus service
Small embeddable core that scales from a CLI script to many microservices
limits: A Java ecosystem: you need a JVM, and Java skills to debug, extend or tune it
Each route runs where you deploy it; there is no central server with back pressure, queues on disk or provenance like NiFi’s, so durability depends on the brokers you route through
The breadth is also a learning curve: hundreds of components, several DSLs and runtimes, and many subprojects to choose between
Frequent releases; staying supported means tracking the LTS lines (in October 2026, 4.18 until February 2027 and 4.22 until August 2027)

story: Gregor Hohpe and Bobby Woolf’s book Enterprise Integration Patterns (Addison-Wesley, 2003) named 65 recurring ways that messages are routed, split, merged and transformed between systems, and spurred a generation of open-source integration products. James Strachan checked in the first code of the Camel routing library on 19 March 2007, inside the Apache ActiveMQ project’s repository: the patterns as a small Java library with a routing DSL, rather than a separate server.

Camel became a top-level Apache project in December 2008. Camel 2.0 followed in August 2009 and 3.0 in November 2019. Camel 4.0, published in August 2023 as a long-term-support release, required Java 17, moved from `javax` to Jakarta EE 10 APIs and targeted Spring Boot 3 and Quarkus 3. The project now ships a feature release roughly every month or two, with two LTS lines supported at a time.

choices.why: Integration usually meant deploying an enterprise service bus; a small library with few dependencies lets the same patterns run inside any Java application, test or container.
A URI names both the component and its options in one string, and the API is the same whatever the transport, so switching from files to S3 or from JMS to Kafka changes the URI, not the route.

choices.choice: Name things after Enterprise Integration Patterns
choices.why: A shared vocabulary from the book makes routes readable across teams, and every DSL uses the same pattern names.
